messages.author: 3b5b69b5e7c80915
messages.subject: How to marginalize latent variable z in supervised LDA?
parts:
supervised LDA is here:
https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/BleiMcAuliffe2007.pdf

It uses the latent variable z (topic index) to calculate document summary vectors which connect the document to some score Y . The reason why it uses not theta but z to characterize documents is in the following pdf at 129 page:
https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/ChangBlei2010.pdf

If Stan allows discrete parameter, I can write the model as follow:

data {
  int<lower=2> K;                    # num topics
  int<lower=2> V;                    # num words
  int<lower=1> M;                    # num docs
  int<lower=1> N;                    # total word instances
  int<lower=1,upper=V> W[N];         # word n
  real Y[M];                         # score m
  int<lower=1,upper=N> Offset[M,2];  # range of word index per doc
  cov_matrix[K] Cov;
}
transformed data {
  vector[K] Zero;
  for (k in 1:K)
    Zero[k] <- 0;
}
parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[K] alpha;     # topic prior
  vector<lower=0>[V] beta;      # word prior
  simplex[K] theta[M];          # topic dist for doc m
  int<lower=1,upper=K> z[N];    # topic index
  simplex[V] phi[K];            # word dist for topic k
  vector[K] eta;
  real eta0;
}
model {
  vector<lower=0>[K] z_bar[M];  # doc summary vector

  # prior
  for (m in 1:M)
    theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);
  for (k in 1:K)
    phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta);

  for (m in 1:M)
    for (k in 1:K)
      z_bar[m,k] <- 0;

  for (m in 1:M) {
    for (n in Offset[m,1]:Offset[m,2]) {
      z[n] ~ categorical(theta[m]);
      W[n] ~ categorical(phi[z[n]]);
      z_bar[m,z[n]] <- z_bar[m,z[n]] + 1;
    }
    z_bar[m] <- z_bar[m]/(Offset[m,2]-Offset[m,1]+1);
  }
  eta ~ multi_normal(Zero, Cov);
  eta0 ~ normal(0, 100);
  for (m in 1:M)
    Y[m] ~ normal(eta0 + dot_product(eta, z_bar[m]), 1.0);
}

But I have no idea how to marginalize out z. Do you have any idea?

Regards,
Be

parts:
I don't see how to do this offhand (someone else may be cleverer).

The problem is that pesky z_bar that depends on the cumulative assignment
to each word's topic. If you did run things just through theta rather than
z_bar, it'd be easy enough. I don't quite undertand the argumentation in
Chang and Blei p. 129 as to why you can't just use theta. Is the problem
that theta will just spread out with part of it used for links and a disjoint
part for words? Using a statistic based on a discrete parameter seems an
odd way to constrain this, but I don't have any experience with these models.
Maybe there's an alternative that's a little more direct?

- Bob

> Dear Bob,

>
> I think I have to count up all the cases of multinomial distribution (N=number of words, Classes=number of topics) to marginalize out z_bar. It's finite, but substantially impossible to count up if N > 1000.

Exactly. We have this same problem if we want
to do variable selection on coefficients for regression
with a discrete parameter.

>
> > Is the problem that theta will just spread out with part of it used for links and a disjoint part for words?
>
> I agree with you. So I'd like to check the differences between theta model and z_bar model by using Stan.
>

I don't see how to compare any of these things given the wildly
multimodal posteriors you wind up getting. It's not really possible
to do proper Bayesian inference in most of these models.

There are some results coming out using spectral methods about
separability in clusters and stability of inference, but I haven't
been keeping up with any of it and don't even know where to point you.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to marginalize latent variable z in supervised LDA?
parts:
On May 17, 2014, at 4:12 PM, Be <heart...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I don't see how to compare any of these things given the wildly
> > multimodal posteriors you wind up getting. It's not really possible
> > to do proper Bayesian inference in most of these models.
>
> I have an experience with comparing such models by reindexing topic indexes so that absolute difference minimizes. I can say it works.
>

What are you comparing for?

If you compare the distributions across chains, you can often
get a few high-probability topics lining up fairly well. But
then if you have K=50 in something like LDA, then only about
20 or 30 have lined up in my experience. I think that's similar
to what Steyvers and Griffiths (2007) found:

Steyvers, Mark and Tom Griffiths.
2007.
Probabilistic topic models.
In Thomas K. Landauer, Danielle S. McNamara, Simon Dennis and
Walter Kintsch (eds.), Handbook of Latent Semantic Analysis. Laurence Erlbaum.

See the section on "topic stability evaluation" in this tutorial I wrote for the last piece of software
I was working on before Stan (LingPipe) [which contains a full ref, too]:

http://alias-i.com/lingpipe/demos/tutorial/cluster/read-me.html

That software follows Steyvers and Griffiths in going the other way,
marginalizing out the continuous parameters.

You can also find well-separated synthetic examples that line
up very well across chains with reindexing. There's also an
example of that following Griffiths and Steyvers' example, too.

> > There are some results coming out using spectral methods about
> > separability in clusters and stability of inference, but I haven't
> > been keeping up with any of it and don't even know where to point you.
>
> I'm sorry. I'd like to check mainly goodness of convergence and prediction performance (of some score Y). I will use some toy data.
>

How do you want to measure convergence of a topic model like
this? A single chain will converge pretty quickly, but even if
you take optimal index reassignment across chains, you won't see
very good convergence by measures like R-hat.

Other alternatives are using some kind of predictive evaluation,
like as a language model for new documents (which also requires
a marginalization, this time over topic distribution and topic
assignments).

- Bob

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Re: How to marginalize latent variable z in supervised LDA?
parts:
It makes no sense to do LDA with Stan, except (maybe) for educational purposes. 

I have lately used Wray Buntine's hca, available in mloss.org. It can do basic LDA as well as more flexible priors. I have not done any quantitative comparisons, but the results are qualitatively, judged from topic "word" assignments, much better with hca than with the online LDA algorithm of Vowpal Wabbit. (Admittedly, I may be missing something important with the parameters of the VW, and the model is not the same, so the comparison is unfair.)

hca estimates by sampling, and the default models are with hierarchical "Pitman-Yor process" priors. (Calling it PYP is technically correct but a bit misleading , for the base measure is finite.)

Although collapsed Gibbs samplers of LDA-like models have no hope of sampling from the true posterior, they may still beat other methods in predictive performance, per CPU unit. Buntine has some comparisons related to this in his slides which I can't currently find by Google.

On May 20, 2014, at 2:42 PM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> It makes no sense to do LDA with Stan, except (maybe) for educational purposes.

I'd say the problem is MCMC, not Stan per se. You can use Stan's
optimizers to fit LDA models with fixed priors.

The other reason to use something like Stan is for playing around
with different priors.

> I have lately used Wray Buntine's hca, available in mloss.org. It can do basic LDA as well as more flexible priors. I have not done any quantitative comparisons, but the results are qualitatively, judged from topic "word" assignments, much better with hca than with the online LDA algorithm of Vowpal Wabbit. (Admittedly, I may be missing something important with the parameters of the VW, and the model is not the same, so the comparison is unfair.)

Matt Hoffman's algorithm in Vowpal Wabbit assumes you have a lot of
data. Or presumably go through the data more than once. I don't know
how VW's implemented there, but Matt obviously will :-)

We're working on generalizing the stochastic VB Matt did to Stan.
Maybe in another six months or a year we'll have something to release.

>
> hca estimates by sampling, and the default models are with hierarchical "Pitman-Yor process" priors. (Calling it PYP is technically correct but a bit misleading , for the base measure is finite.)
Is that something we could or should implement in Stan?

> Although collapsed Gibbs samplers of LDA-like models have no hope of sampling from the true posterior, they may still beat other methods in predictive performance, per CPU unit. Buntine has some comparisons related to this in his slides which I can't currently find by Google.

My own experience is that the inits matter a lot and the priors
on theta and beta matter a lot in terms of where you get to in the end.

My experience in industry is that customers love love love to see LDA output!
I like to present it a bit differently, by looking at something like TF/IDF
ranking of topics (for which I use z-scores) --- it works much better than
raw frequency to summarize topics (though I just pulled it out of thin
air --- there's no real motiviation). See:

http://alias-i.com/lingpipe/demos/tutorial/cluster/read-me.html

- Bob

> I don't know. As a prior for mixture models it could be useful for someone.
>
> As an LDA prior it may be clearly better than symmetric Dirichlet,

Well, we probably wouldn't use a symmetric Dirichlet in any
serious modeling we did (there was a Hannah Wallach paper on
why it's a bad idea for vanilla LDA, too, with demonstrations
of how a more informative prior for natural language could help).
> but the (discrete) sampling scheme seems quite tricky.

We only get finitely many continuous parameters. So we'd need
to marginalize out the discrete part. I don't think that's
possible for Dirichlet processes, but I'm hardly a non-parametrics
algorithm expert (and if I'm wrong and someone can point me to how
to do it, that'd be super useful).

- Bob
